items.title: Plain English: everyday words (Level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Plain English means writing that your reader can understand the first time they read it. Government writers use it because many people who contact a department are busy, worried or new to the subject. GOV.UK guidance says to use everyday words rather than formal or old-fashioned ones. For example, write 'use' instead of 'utilise', 'start' instead of 'commence', 'help' instead of 'facilitate', 'before' instead of 'prior to', 'about' instead of 'approximately', 'send' instead of 'forward', 'need' instead of 'require', 'enough' instead of 'sufficient', and 'if' instead of 'in the event that'. Jargon is specialist language that only people inside one profession or organisation understand. Avoid it, or explain it the first time you use it. Write abbreviations out in full the first time, with the short form in brackets, for example Department for Work and Pensions (DWP). Do not use Latin abbreviations such as 'e.g.' or 'i.e.'. Write 'for example' or 'that is' instead. Plain English is not childish or 'dumbed down'. It is clear, respectful and quick to read, and it works for expert readers as well as beginners.

items.title: Plain English: short sentences (Level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Short sentences are easier to read than long ones. GOV.UK content design guidance says to use sentences of 25 words or fewer and to give each sentence one main idea. Put the main point first so the reader sees it straight away, then add the detail. Tell the reader what they need to do and by when. Use the active voice, where the person or team doing the action comes first: 'The team approved your claim' is clearer than 'Your claim was approved by the team'. Speak to the reader directly with 'you', and use 'we' for your department. Avoid double negatives such as 'it is not uncommon', which make the reader work harder. Keep paragraphs short, with a blank line between them, so that a page does not look like a solid block of text. When you have several separate items, use a bulleted list with a short lead-in line. Finally, read your writing aloud. If you run out of breath, stumble over a phrase, or hear a word that does not earn its place, rewrite it. Ask a colleague to read it too, because a fresh reader spots problems you cannot see.

items.title: Government style: dates, numbers and capitals (Level 1)
items.body: The GOV.UK style guide sets simple rules so that government writing looks consistent. Write dates as '25 December 2025', with no 'th' or 'st' and no commas. Write times as '9am' and '5:30pm', with no space and no full stops, and use 'midday' and 'midnight' instead of 12pm or 12am. For ranges, use 'to', for example '9am to 5pm', not a dash. Write numbers from one to nine in words and numbers from 10 upwards as figures, for example 'seven letters and 12 emails'. Write percentages with the symbol, such as '50%'. Write money with the pound sign, for example '£5', and only add pence when needed, as in '£5.50'. Use sentence case for headings, which means a capital letter only on the first word and on proper nouns: 'How to apply for a passport'. Do not write whole words in capitals, because capitals are harder to read and can look like shouting. Write abbreviations such as UK and BBC without full stops. Link text should describe where the link goes, for example 'Check if you need a visa', not 'click here'.

items.title: Email basics (Level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: Email is the quickest way to contact colleagues and many customers, but it still needs care. The 'To' box holds the person who needs to act. 'Cc' stands for carbon copy and is for people who only need to know. 'Bcc' means blind carbon copy: the people in it receive the email, but nobody else can see their addresses. Use Bcc when you write to a large group who do not know each other, so you do not share their email addresses. The subject line tells the reader what the email is about, so make it specific, for example 'Meeting on Tuesday 4 March: room changed'. Start with a greeting such as 'Dear Ms Patel' or 'Hello Sam', put your main point in the first line, and keep the email short. Finish with a polite sign-off such as 'Kind regards' and your name and job title. Do not use slang or sign-offs such as 'Cheers mate' with members of the public. Before you press send, check the recipients, check that any attachment is really attached, and check spelling. 'Reply all' sends your answer to everyone on the original email, so use it only when everyone needs your answer.

items.title: Letters to the public: the basics (Level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: A letter to a member of the public is often the way a person learns about a decision that affects their life, so it should be clear, polite and complete. A standard letter has the sender's address and contact details, the date, a reference number, the reader's name and address, a greeting, a short heading, the message, a sign-off, and the name and job title of the writer. Quote the reference number so the reader can use it when they reply. If you know the person's name, begin 'Dear Mr Jones' and end 'Yours sincerely'. If you do not know the name and use 'Dear Sir or Madam', end 'Yours faithfully'. Put the main point in the first paragraph, explain what happens next, and say what the reader needs to do and by when. Give contact details so they can ask questions. Use a clear sans serif font such as Arial at 12 point or larger, because small or fancy fonts are hard to read. Keep a copy of every letter you send, so there is a record of what was said. Keep the tone polite, calm and helpful, even if the letter gives bad news.

items.title: Spreadsheets: cells and formulas (Level 1)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: A spreadsheet is a grid for storing and calculating with data. In Excel, a file is called a workbook, and it holds one or more worksheets, also called sheets. Each sheet is made of columns, labelled with letters, and rows, labelled with numbers. Where a column and a row meet is a cell. Each cell has a reference made of its column letter and row number, so the cell in column C and row 4 is C4. A range is a block of cells, written with a colon, so A1:A5 means the five cells from A1 down to A5. To make a calculation, type an equals sign first. Everything that starts with = is treated as a formula. For example, =5+3 shows 8. Use + to add, - to subtract, * to multiply and / to divide. A formula can use cell references: if B2 holds 4 and B3 holds 6, then =B2*B3 shows 24. The cell displays the result, while the formula bar above the grid shows the formula itself. When you change a number in a cell that a formula uses, the result updates automatically. This is why spreadsheets save time and reduce errors compared with working by hand.

questions.hint: Typing = tells the spreadsheet that a formula follows.

items.title: Spreadsheets: simple functions (Level 1)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: A function is a ready-made formula that does a common job. You write its name, then the cells it should use in brackets. SUM adds numbers: =SUM(B2:B6) adds every number from B2 to B6. AVERAGE finds the mean, which is the total divided by how many numbers there are: =AVERAGE(B2:B6). MAX returns the largest number and MIN returns the smallest. COUNT tells you how many cells in the range hold numbers. Imagine cells B2 to B6 hold 4, 8, 6, 10 and 2. Then SUM is 30, AVERAGE is 6, MAX is 10, MIN is 2 and COUNT is 5. The AutoSum button on the Home tab inserts a SUM formula for you, usually guessing the range of numbers next to it. Writing =SUM(A1:A3) gives the same answer as =A1+A2+A3 but is quicker, and it is easier to extend if you add more rows. Function names are not case sensitive, so sum and SUM both work, but every function needs its brackets. If you misspell a function name, Excel shows the error #NAME?.

questions.hint: The total of 30 divided by 5 numbers is 6.

questions.hint: MIN returns the smallest number, which is 2.

questions.hint: AVERAGE gives the mean.

items.title: Spreadsheets: sorting, filtering and formats (Level 1)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Spreadsheets can organise data as well as calculate. Sorting puts rows in order. Sort A to Z puts text in alphabetical order, and sort smallest to largest puts numbers in ascending order, from low to high. Sort largest to smallest is descending order. A filter shows only the rows that meet a condition, such as every row where the department is 'Finance'. The other rows are hidden, not deleted, and they come back when you clear the filter. Filters and sorts work best when the data has a header row, which is the top row with a name for each column, such as Name, Department and Salary. Freeze panes keeps the header row visible as you scroll down a long list. Cell formats change how a value looks without changing the value itself. Currency format adds a £ sign, percentage format shows 0.5 as 50%, and date format shows a number as a date. If a column is too narrow for a number, the cell shows #####. Widening the column fixes this. Always check that your data has no blank rows in the middle, because they can stop sorting and filtering from working on the whole list.

items.title: Security classifications: the three levels (Level 1)
items.body: The UK government uses a system called the Government Security Classifications to decide how to protect its information. It has three levels: OFFICIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET. The scheme replaced an older one with more levels, including RESTRICTED and CONFIDENTIAL, in 2014. OFFICIAL is the lowest level, and most government information, such as routine emails, policy drafts and casework, sits here. It is not for public release, but its loss would not usually cause serious harm. SECRET is for very sensitive information that needs enhanced protection, where loss could seriously harm national security or safety. TOP SECRET is the highest level, for the most sensitive information, where loss could threaten life or national security on a very large scale. Some OFFICIAL information is more sensitive, such as personal data about individuals or commercial details. This can be marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE. This is not a fourth classification. It is a handling caveat, a warning that extra care is needed. The 'need to know' principle means you only share information with people who need it to do their job. Everyone who works for government is responsible for protecting the information they handle.

items.title: Data protection: key words (Level 1)
items.source: ICO guidance on UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018
items.body: Data protection law in the UK is set out in the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. It protects people's personal data. Personal data is any information about an identified or identifiable living person, such as a name, home address, email address, date of birth, National Insurance number or photograph. A person the data is about is called a data subject. A controller decides why and how personal data is used, and government departments are often controllers. The regulator is the Information Commissioner's Office, known as the ICO. Some personal data is more sensitive and is called special category data. It includes information about health, ethnic origin, religion, political opinions, trade union membership, sex life or sexual orientation, genetic data and biometric data used for identification. It needs extra protection. The law sets out seven principles. These include using data lawfully, fairly and transparently, collecting only what you need (data minimisation), keeping data accurate, not keeping it longer than necessary, and keeping it secure. Data subjects also have rights, including the right to see the information held about them. Anyone handling personal data at work must follow these rules.

items.title: Phishing and passwords (Level 1)
items.body: Phishing is when criminals send fake messages to trick you into clicking a link, opening an attachment or giving away information such as passwords. It usually arrives by email. Similar tricks come by text message, which is called smishing, and by phone call, which is called vishing. Warning signs include an unexpected message, pressure to act straight away, threats such as 'your account will be closed', a sender address that looks odd, spelling mistakes, and links that do not go where they claim. Hovering over a link shows the real web address without clicking it. If you suspect a message is phishing, do not click anything or reply. Report it to your security or IT team, using the reporting button or the process your department sets out. Passwords are your first line of defence. The NCSC advises using three random words to make a long password that is easy to remember but hard to guess. Use a different password for each account, because if one is stolen, criminals try it elsewhere. Never share your password with anyone, including colleagues. Multi-factor authentication adds a second check, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: In cyber security, what is phishing?

options.text: Sending large numbers of unwanted advertising emails
Using software to slow down a computer network
Sending fake messages to trick people into clicking or giving away information
Breaking into a building to steal documents

questions.hint: Phishing aims to trick the reader into acting.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common warning sign of a phishing message?

options.text: A reply to an email you wrote earlier
A message sent during office hours
A greeting that uses your full name

questions.hint: Urgency and threats are typical of phishing.

questions.prompt: What should you do with a suspicious email?

options.text: Forward it to colleagues to ask what they think
Report it to your security or IT team without clicking anything
Open the attachment in case it is harmless
Reply to the sender to ask if it is genuine

questions.hint: Reporting lets the experts deal with it and warns others.

questions.prompt: What password approach does the NCSC recommend?

options.text: Your date of birth and your initials
A short word with a number at the end
The same strong password for every account

questions.hint: Three random words make a long, memorable password.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a trusted colleague asks for your password?

options.text: Share it only while you are away from work
Refuse, because passwords must stay personal
Share it through the work email system
Share it if they hold the same clearance

questions.hint: Passwords are personal and should never be shared.

questions.prompt: What is multi-factor authentication?

options.text: A password that has more than one word in it
A system that changes your password every day
A way for several people to share one login
An extra check, such as a code on your phone, as well as a password

questions.hint: MFA means a stolen password alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: What is the name for phishing sent by text message?
questions.hint: Smishing combines SMS and phishing.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to use the same password for several accounts?

options.text: If one account is breached, criminals try the password elsewhere
Websites will not accept a repeated password
The password would be too short to remember
The accounts would be locked after one week

questions.hint: Reused passwords let one breach spread to other accounts.

questions.prompt: What does hovering your mouse over a link let you do?

options.text: See the real web address without clicking
Open the page in a safe mode

questions.hint: Hovering reveals where the link really goes.

items.title: Clear desk, sending and reporting (Level 1)
items.source: Government Security guidance; ICO guidance on personal data breaches
items.body: Good habits protect information every day. A clear desk policy means you do not leave papers, notes or devices where others could see or take them. When you leave your desk, even briefly, lock your computer screen. On Windows you can press the Windows key and L together. At the end of the day, lock papers and devices away. Put paper with personal or sensitive information in the confidential waste bin or shredder, not in ordinary recycling. Never write passwords on sticky notes. If you see someone you do not recognise in the office without a pass, politely ask who they are and who they are visiting, and tell security if you are unsure. When you send information, check the address before you press send, because sending to the wrong person is one of the most common causes of data breaches. A personal data breach is a security incident that leads to personal data being lost, destroyed, altered, shared or accessed by someone who should not have it. If you spot or cause a breach, tell your line manager and your data protection or security team straight away. Do not try to hide it. Organisations must tell the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach that is likely to risk people's rights.

questions.prompt: What should you do when you leave your desk, even briefly?

options.text: Turn the monitor off at the plug
Save your files to a memory stick

questions.hint: Locking the screen stops others seeing or using your session.

questions.prompt: Which keys lock a Windows computer screen quickly?
questions.hint: Windows key plus L locks the screen.

questions.prompt: Where should paper with personal details go when you no longer need it?

options.text: In the confidential waste or shredder
In a drawer that is left unlocked
In your bag to take home

questions.hint: Confidential waste keeps personal data from being read by others.

questions.prompt: What should you do with papers at the end of the day?

options.text: Leave them tidy on the desk

questions.hint: A clear desk means papers are locked away.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a safe place to keep a password?

options.text: In a password manager approved by your department
On a sticky note on your monitor

questions.hint: Notes on a desk can be read by anyone.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you sent an email to the wrong person?

options.text: Wait to see if the recipient replies
Send a second email asking them to delete the first
Delete it from your Sent folder
Tell your line manager and the data protection team straight away

questions.hint: Reporting quickly lets the organisation limit the harm.

questions.prompt: Within how many hours must a reportable breach be notified to the ICO?
questions.hint: The limit is 72 hours from becoming aware of the breach.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you see a stranger without a pass in the office?

options.text: Ignore them, as security will notice
Ask them to sign your visitor book
Politely ask who they are and report it if unsure
Let them stay unless they ask for help

questions.hint: Challenging politely, and telling security, protects the building.

questions.prompt: What is a personal data breach?

options.text: A security incident where personal data is lost, shared or accessed wrongly
A request from a person to see their data
A planned update to a computer system
Any complaint made about how a department behaves

questions.hint: Breaches involve personal data going to the wrong place or being lost.
